title: Ash Wednesday (Joel 2:12–18)
hook: rend your hearts and not your garments

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette, where the wheelchairs lead the procession. Your line was the sick come first.

On one Wednesday every year, people walk around cities with a dark smudge on their foreheads: on the subway, at the office, in the grocery line. Coworkers lean in and say, you've got something on your face. It isn't a holy day of obligation; nobody is required to go. And yet people line up, at lunch hour, before work, after school, to be told in ash that they are dust. Lent starts here.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE SUBWAY.` → `NOT REQUIRED, YET THEY COME.` → `LENT STARTS HERE.`

segments.voice: The first reading is the prophet Joel. A disaster has hit the land, a plague of locusts, and Joel calls the whole people to turn back to God with fasting, weeping and mourning. Then the line that keeps it from becoming theater. In the Douay-Rheims: "And rend your hearts, and not your garments." In the ancient world, tearing your clothes was the public sign of grief; Joel says tear the inside instead. Then the reason to hope: God is gracious and merciful, patient and rich in mercy. Joel even calls the newlyweds out of their wedding chamber; nobody is too busy for this. The gospel, from Matthew 6, says almost the same: when you give, pray or fast, do it in secret, and wash your face so no one can tell. And then everyone goes up and gets a visible mark on their face. The Church holds that tension on purpose. The ashes are made by burning last year's palms from Palm Sunday. The priest marks a cross and says one of two things: Repent, and believe in the Gospel. Or the older words from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast today, one full meal, and those fourteen and up skip meat. This week walked from Christmas into Lent: three gifts, the season ending in water, that they may be one, the persecutor turned, a light to the nations, the sick come first.
screen: `JOEL: LOCUSTS AND A CALL.` · `TEAR THE INSIDE, NOT THE CLOTH.` · `IN SECRET, YET MARKED.` · `ASHES OF LAST YEAR'S PALMS.` · then, large: `DUST THOU ART.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that takes more of you than it should, a habit, a screen, a snack, a tone of voice, and quietly let it go for Lent, or even just this week. The hard part is telling no one: no posts, no announcements, just between you and God, or between you and yourself. If you pray, offer it; either way, rend your heart a little, not your garments.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, when Catholics receive ashes on the forehead and hear: remember that you are dust. Today's word.
Your line: rend your hearts. The inside comes first, the ash second. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics receive ashes on the forehead, made from the previous year's blessed palms, and keep a day of fasting and abstinence from meat; it is not a holy day of obligation.
